<text:col value="10"><text:style bold="true" underlined="true" italic="true">Guida TTCAM</text:style></text:col>
TTCAM is a CAM software written for small/home CNC like CNC 3018. It has several features:
<text:bullet><text:a xlink:href="#1">Rounded Square</text:a></text:bullet>
<text:bullet><text:a xlink:href="#2">Circle</text:a></text:bullet>
<text:bullet><text:a xlink:href="#3">Line</text:a></text:bullet>
<text:bullet><text:a xlink:href="#4">Text</text:a></text:bullet>
<text:bullet><text:a xlink:href="#5">PCB</text:a></text:bullet>
<text:bullet><text:a xlink:href="#6">SVG</text:a></text:bullet>
<text:bullet><text:a xlink:href="#7">Allen Screw</text:a></text:bullet>
<text:bullet><text:a xlink:href="#8">Laser Picture</text:a></text:bullet>
<text:bullet><text:a xlink:href="#9">Sculpting a picture</text:a></text:bullet>
<text:bullet><text:a xlink:href="#10">Working with Elements (Add / Remove / Modify)</text:a></text:bullet>
<text:bullet><text:a xlink:href="#11">Move, Rotate and Pattern (Transform Tools)</text:a></text:bullet>
<text:bullet><text:a xlink:href="#12">Direct GCode Insertion</text:a></text:bullet>
<text:bullet><text:a xlink:href="#13">Projects and GCode Export</text:a></text:bullet>
<text:bullet><text:a xlink:href="#14">Navigating the 2D/3D View</text:a></text:bullet>
<text:bullet><text:a xlink:href="#15">File Preview, Export and Project Comments</text:a></text:bullet>

There are parameters common to almost all features:

<image:base64 col="13" width="50" wrap="center"></image:base64>

<text:style bold="true">Movement & Speed Parameters</text:style>

	<text:style bold="true">Rapid feed rate</text:style>
		What it does: Controls the maximum speed of the machine when the tool moves "in the air" without cutting.
		Purpose: It minimizes idle time between different cutting operations (triggered by the G0 G-code command).
  
	<text:style bold="true">Feed rate XY</text:style>
		What it does: The horizontal speed of the tool while it is actively cutting into the material.
		Purpose: It determines surface finish; setting it too high breaks the bit, while setting it too low can burn the material.

	<text:style bold="true">Feed Rate Z</text:style>
		What it does: The vertical speed at which the tool plunges downward into the material.
		Purpose: This is usually much slower than the XY feed rate because router bits handle vertical compression stress poorly.

	<text:style bold="true">Spindle Speed</text:style>
		What it does: The rotational speed of the motor holding the bit, measured in Revolutions Per Minute (RPM).
		Purpose: It must be balanced with feed rates based on the material; metals need low RPM, while plastics or wood require high RPM.

<text:style bold="true">Geometry & Cutting Parameters</text:style>

	<text:style bold="true">Tool diameter</text:style>
		What it does: The exact width/thickness of the physical router bit you are using.
		Purpose: The CAM software uses this to calculate tool radius compensation, preventing the machine from cutting too deep into your final part shape.

	<text:style bold="true">Finish Allowance</text:style>
		What it does: Specifies a small thickness of material that the software intentionally leaves uncut during the initial roughing passes.
		Purpose: This extra material is removed in a final "finishing pass" to achieve perfect dimensions and a smooth surface.

	<text:style bold="true"> Max Ramp Angle</text:style>
		What it does: Defines the maximum angle (in degrees) at which the tool enters the material diagonally instead of plunging straight down.
		Purpose: It avoids the harsh "drill-like" vertical impact, reducing stress on the tool tip and extending its lifespan.

<text:style bold="true">Depth & Work Coordinate Parameters</text:style>

	<text:style bold="true">ZStart</text:style>
			What it does: The coordinate representing the very top surface of the raw material.
			Purpose: It tells the machine where the actual cutting begins so it can calculate depth correctly.

	<text:style bold="true">ZDepth</text:style>
		What it does: The total final depth that the cut or pocket needs to reach relative to your Z-zero.
		Purpose: It determines how deep a pocket is or ensures the tool cuts all the way through a panel.

    <text:style bold="true">ZStep</text:style>
		What it does: The maximum depth the machine is allowed to cut down in a single horizontal pass (also called depth of cut).
		Purpose: If you need to cut 10 mm deep (ZDepth) with a 2 mm ZStep, the machine will safely make 5 progressive passes to avoid overloading the motor.

<text:style bold="true">Strategies & Special Modes</text:style>

	<text:style bold="true"> Direction (Conventional/Climb)</text:style>
		What it does: Chooses the rotation direction of the cutter relative to the direction of the tool movement.
		Climb: The tool "bites" the material from top to bottom, yielding a superior finish and less tool wear (the standard choice for rigid industrial CNCs).
		Conventional: The tool pushes against the material, which is ideal for less rigid hobbyist machines to prevent mechanical play (backlash) from pulling the carriage.

	<text:style bold="true">Laser Mode (On/Off)</text:style>

		What it does: Enables or disables dedicated control commands for laser engraving or cutting heads instead of a spindle.
		Purpose: When turned On, the G-code dynamically scales the laser power based on machine acceleration (M3/M4), preventing scorched corners when the machine slows down to turn.
		
<text:style bold="true">Rounded Square</text:style><text:bookmark text:name="1"/>
<image:base64 col="0" width="10" wrap="center"></image:base64>
Description of the fields

	<text:style bold="true">X, Y</text:style>
		What it does: The coordinates of the reference corner of the rectangle (before rounding).
		Purpose: Positions the shape on the working area.

	<text:style bold="true">Width, Height</text:style>
		What it does: The size of the rectangle along X and Y.
		Purpose: Defines the overall footprint of the shape to cut or engrave.

	<text:style bold="true">Radius</text:style>
		What it does: The radius applied to the four corners of the rectangle.
		Purpose: Set it to 0 for a sharp square/rectangle, or to any value up to half of the shortest side to obtain rounded corners.

	<text:style bold="true">Thickness</text:style>
		What it does: When greater than 0, only the outline (a frame of this thickness) is machined instead of the full area.
		Purpose: Use 0 to cut/pocket the whole rectangle; use a value greater than 0 to engrave or cut only the border, leaving the inside untouched.

	<text:style bold="true">Compensation</text:style>
		What it does: Offsets the toolpath by the tool radius: None (no offset, the tool centre follows the drawn geometry), Int (the path is shifted inward by half the tool diameter) or Ext (the path is shifted outward by half the tool diameter).
		Purpose: Int is normally used to cut a pocket or a hole to the exact drawn size; Ext is normally used to cut an external profile (for example to obtain a part exactly Width x Height once cut out).

	<text:style bold="true">Advanced</text:style>
		What it does: Opens the Transformation Matrix, a 2x3 affine matrix ([a b c / d e f]) that is applied to the shape after it has been generated.
		Purpose: Allows scaling, rotating, shearing or skewing the element beyond the simple parameters above, for advanced users who need full geometric control.


<text:style bold="true">Circle</text:style><text:bookmark text:name="2"/>
<image:base64 col="0" width="10" wrap="center"></image:base64>
Description of the fields

	<text:style bold="true">X, Y</text:style>
		What it does: The coordinates of the centre of the circle.
		Purpose: Positions the circle on the working area.

	<text:style bold="true">Radius</text:style>
		What it does: The radius of the circle.
		Purpose: Sets the overall size of the disc, ring or hole to be machined.

	<text:style bold="true">Thickness</text:style>
		What it does: When greater than 0, only a ring of this thickness is machined instead of the full disc.
		Purpose: Use 0 to mill a full disc/pocket; use a value greater than 0 to cut only a ring (for example to engrave a circle outline, or to cut a washer).

	<text:style bold="true">Compensation</text:style>
		What it does: Same as for the Rounded Square: None, Int (offset inward by the tool radius) or Ext (offset outward by the tool radius).
		Purpose: Int is typically used for holes/pockets machined to size; Ext is typically used to cut a circular part out of the stock.

	<text:style bold="true">Advanced</text:style>
		What it does: Opens the same Transformation Matrix described for the Rounded Square.
		Purpose: Lets you turn the circle into an ellipse or apply any other affine transformation.


<text:style bold="true">Line</text:style><text:bookmark text:name="3"/>
<image:base64 col="0" width="10" wrap="center"></image:base64>
Description of the fields

	<text:style bold="true">X1, Y1</text:style>
		What it does: The coordinates of the starting point of the segment.
		Purpose: Defines where the tool starts following the line.

	<text:style bold="true">X2, Y2</text:style>
		What it does: The coordinates of the ending point of the segment.
		Purpose: Defines where the line ends, together with X1/Y1 it sets length and direction.

	<text:style bold="true">Thickness</text:style>
		What it does: When greater than 0, the line is machined as a slot of this width instead of a single toolpath along the centre line.
		Purpose: Use 0 for a simple engraved/scored line following the tool centre; use a value greater than 0 to cut a slot wider than the tool diameter.


<text:style bold="true">Text</text:style><text:bookmark text:name="4"/>
<image:base64 col="0" width="10" wrap="center"></image:base64>
Description of the fields

	<text:style bold="true">X, Y</text:style>
		What it does: The coordinates of the insertion point of the text.
		Purpose: Positions the text on the working area.

	<text:style bold="true">Size</text:style>
		What it does: The height of the characters, in the same unit used by the rest of the project (mm).
		Purpose: Controls how large the engraved/cut text will be.

	<text:style bold="true">Text</text:style>
		What it does: The actual string to engrave or cut.
		Purpose: This is the content that will be converted into toolpaths, character by character.

	<text:style bold="true">Font</text:style>
		What it does: Selects which installed system font is used to build the letter outlines.
		Purpose: Different fonts produce different stroke shapes; choose a simple, single-line-friendly font for engraving with small tools, since very thin or decorative fonts may be hard to reproduce with a router bit.

		Note: the Common parameters (Feed rate, Z Depth, Tool diameter, etc.) apply exactly as described above; there is no additional Compensation option because text outlines are engraved/cut following the tool centre line.


<text:style bold="true">PCB</text:style><text:bookmark text:name="5"/>
<image:base64 col="0" width="10" wrap="center"></image:base64>
The PCB tool converts a bitmap image of a printed circuit board layout into isolation-routing and drilling toolpaths.

Description of the fields

	<text:style bold="true">X, Y</text:style>
		What it does: The coordinates of the reference corner (top-left) where the image is placed.
		Purpose: Positions the imported board on the working area.

	<text:style bold="true">DPI</text:style>
		What it does: The resolution (dots per inch) the source image was exported at.
		Purpose: It is used to convert the image from pixels to real-world millimetres, so the resulting board has the correct physical size.

	<text:style bold="true">Traces</text:style>
		What it does: Enables/disables the generation of the isolation-routing toolpath around the copper traces.
		Purpose: Turn it on to actually engrave the isolation channels between copper tracks and pads.

	<text:style bold="true">Expand Traces</text:style>
		What it does: Grows (or shrinks, with a negative value) the copper areas by this amount before the isolation path is computed.
		Purpose: Compensates for the width of the engraving tool, so the remaining copper track keeps a safe width and adjacent tracks do not merge.

	<text:style bold="true">Auto Hole (red pads)</text:style>
		What it does: When enabled, every pad marked in pure red in the source image is automatically turned into a drilled hole.
		Purpose: Saves the manual step of adding an Allen Screw/hole element for every component pad; the drill diameter and depth are taken from the two fields below.

	<text:style bold="true">Max Holes dia</text:style>
		What it does: The diameter of the drill used for the automatic pad holes.
		Purpose: Should match the drill bit actually mounted on the machine for drilling component holes/vias.

	<text:style bold="true">Holes Depth</text:style>
		What it does: The Z depth reached while drilling the automatic pad holes.
		Purpose: Should be deep enough to go through the board thickness (plus a small safety margin).

	<text:style bold="true">File</text:style>
		What it does: Selects the source bitmap of the board layout.
		Purpose: The image must follow a strict colour convention so the tool can tell traces from pads from bare board: copper traces must be pure black RGB(0,0,0), drill pads must be pure red RGB(255,0,0), and every area that must stay untouched must be pure white RGB(255,255,255).


<text:style bold="true">SVG</text:style><text:bookmark text:name="6"/>
<image:base64 col="0" width="10" wrap="center"></image:base64>
The SVG tool imports a vector drawing and turns every black-filled shape into an engraving/cutting toolpath. It is the most flexible way to bring in complex artwork, logos or technical drawings produced with any vector editor (Inkscape, Illustrator, etc.).

Description of the fields

	<text:style bold="true">X, Y</text:style>
		What it does: The coordinates of the reference corner where the SVG drawing is placed.
		Purpose: Positions the imported vector artwork on the working area.

	<text:style bold="true">Scale factor</text:style>
		What it does: A multiplier applied to the whole drawing size as read from the SVG file.
		Purpose: Lets you resize the artwork without having to edit the original file (1.00 keeps the original SVG size).

	<text:style bold="true">Compensation</text:style>
		What it does: Same tool-radius compensation described for Rounded Square/Circle: None, Int or Ext.
		Purpose: Choose Int/Ext when the filled shapes must be cut to their exact drawn size once the tool diameter is taken into account.

	<text:style bold="true">Engraving mode</text:style>
		What it does: Chooses the strategy used to fill each solid black area: Zig Zag (parallel back-and-forth passes, fastest), Contour (the area is filled with successive offset outlines following its shape) or Concentric (Slow) (concentric offset passes, smoothest finish but slower).
		Purpose: Zig Zag is the quickest general-purpose choice; Contour/Concentric follow the shape of the artwork more faithfully and can give a better surface finish on organic shapes, at the cost of longer machining time.

	<text:style bold="true">File</text:style>
		What it does: Selects the source .svg file.
		Purpose: Only the areas filled with solid black (fill="black") are engraved/cut; anything not filled in black is ignored, so prepare the drawing accordingly before importing it.


<text:style bold="true">Allen Screw</text:style><text:bookmark text:name="7"/>
<image:base64 col="0" width="10" wrap="center"></image:base64>
This tool machines the counterbore/spot-face seat typically needed for a socket-head (Allen) cap screw: a wide, flat-bottomed recess for the screw head, concentric with a narrower hole for the screw shank.

Description of the fields

	<text:style bold="true">X Center, Y Center</text:style>
		What it does: The coordinates of the centre of the hole.
		Purpose: Positions the screw seat on the working area.

	<text:style bold="true">DiameterMajor</text:style>
		What it does: The diameter of the wide counterbore, sized to fit the screw head (with clearance).
		Purpose: Lets the screw head sit flush with, or below, the surface of the material.

	<text:style bold="true">DepthMajor</text:style>
		What it does: How deep the wide counterbore (DiameterMajor) is machined, measured from the top surface (Z Start).
		Purpose: Should be at least equal to the screw head height so the head can be fully recessed.

	<text:style bold="true">DiameterMinor</text:style>
		What it does: The diameter of the narrower, deeper hole for the screw shank/thread, machined below the counterbore down to the Common Z Depth.
		Purpose: Should match the screw shank diameter (through hole) or the recommended tap/pilot diameter (blind, threaded hole).

		Note: this single tool covers the common hole variants used with cap screws simply by adjusting these values together with the Common Z Depth: a plain through hole (DiameterMajor = DiameterMinor, DepthMajor = 0), a countersunk hole (small DepthMajor with a wide DiameterMajor), a blind hole (Z Depth less than the material thickness) or a full flat-bottom counterbore as shown above.


<text:style bold="true">Laser Picture</text:style><text:bookmark text:name="8"/>
<image:base64 col="0" width="10" wrap="center"></image:base64>
This tool converts a photo or grayscale image directly into laser engraving moves, reproducing shades of grey as different amounts of laser power (or a different number of passes) instead of building a cut/engrave outline.

Description of the fields

	<text:style bold="true">X, Y</text:style>
		What it does: The coordinates of the reference corner where the picture is placed.
		Purpose: Positions the engraved picture on the working area.

	<text:style bold="true">Width</text:style>
		What it does: The width the picture will have once engraved; the height is scaled automatically to keep the original picture proportions.
		Purpose: Sets the physical size of the finished engraving.

	<text:style bold="true">Gamma</text:style>
		What it does: A curve applied to every pixel before it is turned into laser power. Gamma = 1 maps grey level to power in a straight line; values above 1 push mid-tones towards Min Power (only the darkest areas approach Max Power); values below 1 push mid-tones towards Max Power.
		Purpose: Lets the engraving contrast be tuned to how the material actually reacts to the laser, without editing the source picture.

	<text:style bold="true">Min Power</text:style>
		What it does: The laser power used for the lightest tones of the picture (near-white).
		Purpose: Sets the baseline energy applied across the whole picture, including its palest areas, so the lightest parts still come out marked instead of untouched.

	<text:style bold="true">Max Power</text:style>
		What it does: The laser power used for the darkest tones of the picture (near-black).
		Purpose: Sets the strongest energy used, for the deepest/darkest marks; every pixel in between is given a power between Min Power and Max Power, scaled to its grey level (and reshaped by Gamma).

	<text:style bold="true">Crosshatch</text:style>
		What it does: None engraves the picture with a single set of parallel passes. 45 Degrees and 90 Degrees add a second full pass at a 45 degrees or 90 degrees angle to the first, engraving the picture twice from two different directions.
		Purpose: The crossed second pass blends adjacent scan lines together, reducing the visible striping of a single-direction scan for a smoother, more photographic result, at the cost of roughly doubling the machining time.

	<text:style bold="true">File</text:style>
		What it does: Selects the source picture (photo or grayscale image).
		Purpose: The image is scanned line by line and converted into laser moves; darker pixels receive more energy (higher power and/or more passes) than lighter pixels.

		Note: selecting this tool automatically switches on Laser mode. In the Common panel, Z Step is replaced by Number of passes (how many times the laser scans over the image, useful for deep/dark engravings); the Common panel's Laser power field is not used by this tool, since the engraving power is controlled by Min Power and Max Power above instead.


<text:style bold="true">Sculpting a picture</text:style><text:bookmark text:name="9"/>
<image:base64 col="0" width="10" wrap="center"></image:base64>
This tool turns a grayscale image into a 3D relief (bas-relief) toolpath, carving the material at a different depth for every pixel according to its brightness, in the same way a heightmap works in 3D software.

Description of the fields

	<text:style bold="true">X, Y</text:style>
		What it does: The coordinates of the reference corner where the relief is placed.
		Purpose: Positions the carved picture on the working area.

	<text:style bold="true">Width</text:style>
		What it does: The width the relief will have once carved; the height is scaled automatically to keep the original picture proportions.
		Purpose: Sets the physical size of the finished relief.

	<text:style bold="true">CrossHatch</text:style>
		What it does: When enabled, the surface is machined twice, once along each axis (a first pass along X, a second pass along Y), instead of a single set of parallel passes.
		Purpose: Removes the small ridges left between adjacent passes, giving a noticeably smoother 3D surface at the cost of roughly doubling the machining time.

	<text:style bold="true">File</text:style>
		What it does: Selects the source grayscale image used as the height map.
		Purpose: White pixels correspond to Z Start (the top surface, left untouched) and black pixels correspond to Z Depth (the deepest point); every shade of grey in between is mapped to a proportional depth, so the picture must be prepared in grayscale before importing it.


<text:style bold="true">Working with Elements (Add / Remove / Modify)</text:style><text:bookmark text:name="10"/>
Every tool described above works the same way: choose the tool from the toolbar, fill in its parameters and the Common parameters, then use the buttons under the Common panel to manage it in the project.

	<text:style bold="true">Add</text:style>
		What it does: Creates a new element with the current parameters and appends it to the Elements List.
		Purpose: This is how every shape, text, picture or hole actually becomes part of the project; the corresponding GCode is generated immediately and shown in the code panel on the right, and the shape appears in the 2D/3D preview.

	<text:style bold="true">Modify</text:style>
		What it does: Applies the current parameter values to the element that is currently selected in the Elements List, instead of creating a new one.
		Purpose: Lets you edit an element you already added, for example to fine-tune its position or depth after seeing it in the preview.

	<text:style bold="true">Remove</text:style>
		What it does: Deletes the element currently selected in the Elements List from the project.
		Purpose: Removes unwanted or mistaken elements; the GCode and the preview are updated immediately.

	<text:style bold="true">Elements List</text:style>
		What it does: Shows every element added to the project so far, in the order they will be machined.
		Purpose: Click an entry to select it: its parameters are reloaded on the left so you can inspect or Modify it, and it is highlighted in the 2D/3D preview.

		Note: every element that produces a toolpath must have a valid Z Depth (and, where relevant, a Tool diameter/Feed rate). Add refuses to create the element and shows an explanatory message (naming the element type and its position in the list) until the missing value is filled in.


<text:style bold="true">Move, Rotate and Pattern (Transform Tools)</text:style><text:bookmark text:name="11"/>
These three tools do not create new geometry by themselves: they duplicate one or more existing elements from the Elements List, applying a translation, a rotation or a fully custom formula, N times in a row. They are the fastest way to create bolt circles, grids, or any other repeated pattern without adding every copy by hand.

<image:base64 col="0" width="10" wrap="center"></image:base64>
	<text:style bold="true">Translate</text:style>
		What it does: Creates N copies of the selected element(s), each one shifted by X, Y with respect to the previous copy (an optional Rotate (degrees) around Pivot X/Pivot Y can be applied at the same time).
		Purpose: Quickly builds linear arrays, for example a row of equally spaced holes.

<image:base64 col="0" width="10" wrap="center"></image:base64>
	<text:style bold="true">Rotate</text:style>
		What it does: Creates N copies of the selected element(s), each one rotated by Rotate (degrees) around Pivot X/Pivot Y with respect to the previous copy (an X/Y offset can be combined with the rotation).
		Purpose: Quickly builds circular/radial patterns, for example a bolt circle of equally spaced screw holes.

<image:base64 col="0" width="10" wrap="center"></image:base64>
	<text:style bold="true">Pattern</text:style>
		What it does: The advanced version of the two tools above: X, Y, Rotate (degrees), Pivot X and Pivot Y are entered as Formulas (mathematical expressions) instead of fixed numbers, and can use the current repetition index N.
		Purpose: Enables patterns that a simple linear or radial step cannot describe, such as spirals or progressively growing/shrinking spacing, by writing a formula that depends on N.

	<text:style bold="true">Common fields</text:style>
		What it does: FOR N going from ... to ... sets how many repetitions are generated (the first and last value of the index N); Apply to selects which element(s) of the Elements List the transform is applied to.
		Purpose: Together they define how many copies are produced and which existing geometry is being repeated.


<text:style bold="true">Direct GCode Insertion</text:style><text:bookmark text:name="12"/>
<image:base64 col="0" width="10" wrap="center"></image:base64>
This tool does not draw any geometry: it inserts a block of raw GCode at a specific point in the machining sequence, in between the elements that precede and follow it in the Elements List.

Description of the fields

	<text:style bold="true">M5 / G0 Z5 / G0 X0 Y0 (Go home)</text:style>
		What it does: Stops the spindle, lifts the tool to a safe height and sends it back to the machine origin.
		Purpose: Handy at the end of a job, or before an operation that requires repositioning the stock.

	<text:style bold="true">M5 / M0 (Pause)</text:style>
		What it does: Stops the spindle and pauses the program unconditionally until the operator resumes it.
		Purpose: Useful to stop and check the work, change the tool, or flip/reposition the workpiece halfway through a job.

	<text:style bold="true">M5 / M1 (conditional pause)</text:style>
		What it does: Stops the spindle and pauses the program only if the "optional stop" function is enabled on the controller.
		Purpose: Same use as the unconditional pause above, but it can be skipped without editing the GCode, simply by disabling optional stop on the machine.

	<text:style bold="true">Customized</text:style>
		What it does: Enables the Customized GCode text box below, where any sequence of GCode lines can be typed freely.
		Purpose: Gives full control for anything not covered by the three preset options above, for example a tool change command, a custom message, or machine-specific GCode.


<text:style bold="true">Projects and GCode Export</text:style><text:bookmark text:name="13"/>
All the elements added to a job form a project, available from the File menu.

	<text:style bold="true">Open Project</text:style>
		What it does: Loads a previously saved project file, restoring its full Elements List.
		Purpose: Resume editing a job that was started earlier.

	<text:style bold="true">Save project / Save as...</text:style>
		What it does: Saves the current Elements List to a project file (Save as... lets you choose the file name/location).
		Purpose: Keeps the editable project (all the elements with their parameters) so it can be reopened and modified later, as opposed to the finished GCode which is no longer editable as elements.

	<text:style bold="true">Export GCode</text:style>
		What it does: Writes the GCode currently shown in the code panel to a .nc/.gcode file.
		Purpose: Produces the final file to load into the CNC controller (for example on the CNC 3018) in order to actually run the job.


<text:style bold="true">Navigating the 2D/3D View</text:style><text:bookmark text:name="14"/>
The panel on the top right shows every element of the project as soon as it is added, and the panel below it shows the corresponding generated GCode, line by line.

	<text:style bold="true">Mouse wheel</text:style>
		What it does: Zooms the view in and out.

	<text:style bold="true">Central mouse button (drag)</text:style>
		What it does: Pans the view.

	<text:style bold="true">Left mouse button (drag)</text:style>
		What it does: Rotates the view in 3D, to inspect depths and ramps from any angle.

	<text:style bold="true">Double left click</text:style>
		What it does: Resets the view to the default top-down position.

		Note: the red and green lines crossing the view are the X and Y axes of the machine origin (0,0); every element coordinate is relative to this origin.

<text:style bold="true">File Preview, Export and Project Comments</text:style><text:bookmark text:name="15"/>
For the PCB, SVG, Laser Picture and Sculpt features, the File menu offers extra tools tied to the source file and to the project itself.

	<text:style bold="true">View Resource</text:style>
		What it does: Opens a preview window showing the image/vector file currently assigned (via the File field) to the selected element, at high resolution, with its size (pixels or mm) and file size overlaid in a corner. Available only when a PCB, SVG, Laser Picture or Sculpt element is selected and a file has been chosen for it.
		Purpose: Check that the correct file was loaded, and how it actually looks, without leaving TTCAM or opening another program.

	<text:style bold="true">Export... (inside the File Preview window)</text:style>
		What it does: Saves a copy of the file shown in the preview window to any location chosen by the user.
		Purpose: Recover the exact resource file used by a project element, even if the original file has since been moved, renamed or deleted, since the file is also embedded inside the .ttcam project when it is saved.

	<text:style bold="true">Comment</text:style>
		What it does: Opens a free text note editor for the whole project; the text is saved inside the .ttcam file when the project is saved (Save / Save as...), and is loaded back automatically the next time the project is opened.
		Purpose: Keep notes together with the project itself, for example what a job is for, machine settings used, or things left to do.
